# 🧱 mBlock beginner examples: Pathfinder 8-Way

[🔙 Back to the Pathfinder 8-Way product page](/en/sensors/line8/index.md)

This page is for people who have **never written a program**: read the Pathfinder 8-Way on an **mBot** with mBlock 5 blocks. The 5 examples start with "turn the number into a sound" and work up to a robot that drives itself. Every example has a block picture, a downloadable project file and an Arduino sketch that does the same thing.

| Software | Who it suits | How to open the example file |
|---|---|---|
| 🟧 **mBlock 5 desktop** (blocks, Upload mode) + **MBC Pro Sensors extension v2** | Schools, first time with an mBot | Download the `.mblock` → open mBlock 5 → "File → Open from your computer" → switch to "Upload" at the bottom right → "Upload" |
| 🔧 **Arduino IDE** (text code) | People who want to see what is behind the blocks, or write their own code | Download the `.ino` → install the Makeblock and MBC_Sensors libraries (see [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md)) → board Arduino Uno → upload |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - The sensor must be the **Makeblock edition with the 2026-10 protocol v2 firmware**, connected through the **mBot socket board** to an RJ25 port; use extension **v2.0.0** (old firmware goes with the old v1 extension; they cannot be mixed).
> - The board is the **mBot (mCore)**. mBot Ranger, Orion and MegaPi work too: swap "when mBot starts up" for that board's hat block and use a port that board allows (see [supported boards and ports](/en/makeblock.md)); the mBot2 (CyberPi) has no RJ25 port and is not supported.
> - mBlock 5 is shown here with its English block text; your copy may show the same blocks in another language.

## Before you start

<figure class="ref-fig"><img src="/images/figures/line8/wiring-mbot.svg" alt="Pathfinder 8-Way × mBot wiring" loading="lazy"></figure>

Sensor → mBot socket board → RJ25 port on the board (S1 = host TX, S2 = host RX, UART 38400).

1. **Install the extension**: get the **MBC Pro Sensors v2.0.0** `.mext` from [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md) and drop it into the mBlock 5 window; add **mBot** under "Devices" (bottom left) and switch to "Upload" (bottom right).
2. **Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1** (every example on this page uses this port; to use another, change the port number on the blocks).
3. **Let it boot first**: every example starts with "wait 1 seconds" so the sensor can boot; reading too early gives -32768 (nothing received yet).
4. **Calibrate once**: with the sensor plugged in and the mBot on, **press and release** the calibration button on the sensor, then within the **5 s** the green LED is on sweep the sensor back and forth across the black line and white surface (all 8 spots must see both). Green LED off = done; it is stored in the sensor. The block "Pathfinder port 1 5-second auto calibration" does the same.
5. **How do you know it worked?** Run example 2: on plain white the LED goes off (line width 0); over the black line it lights.

## Blocks used on this page

Each reporter block is one "value id" of the sensor's value table (the same ids as the Arduino I2C registers); the full block list is in [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md).

| Block | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Pathfinder port [1] fine line position | -100~+100 | sub-channel position: −100 to +100, 0 = centre, negative = left (same sign as line position) |
| Pathfinder port [1] line width | 0~8 路 | number of channels on the line, 0~8; 0 = no line |
| Pathfinder port [1] line position | -8~+8 | which channel the line is under: −8 (far left) to +8 (far right), 0 = centre; seen from behind the robot, negative = left |

**Examples on this page**

1. [Hear where the line is](#example-1-hear-where-the-line-is)
2. [The LED shows which side the line is on](#example-2-the-led-shows-which-side-the-line-is-on)
3. [The line position drives one wheel](#example-3-the-line-position-drives-one-wheel)
4. [Three-way line following](#example-4-three-way-line-following)
5. [Proportional line following + stop when the line is lost](#example-5-proportional-line-following-stop-when-the-line-is-lost)

> [!NOTE]
> The `.mblock` files are generated in the mBlock 5 save format and **have not yet been opened in mBlock 5 for verification** (pending the extension v2 release). If one will not open or shows blank blocks, check that extension v2 is loaded and the device is mBot, or rebuild it from the block picture below (under 5 minutes); you can also [tell us on LINE](https://line.me/R/ti/p/@692vcvuk).

## Example 1: Hear where the line is

**What this example does**: The mBot has no screen, so this example turns the "fine line position" (−100 to +100) into a pitch: 440 Hz (A) with the line in the centre, lower to the left and higher to the right. Learn to "read the number" first; the line-following examples build on it.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- Pathfinder 8-Way (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board
- A white mat with a black line (about 2 cm wide)

**Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1**. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex01_hear_line.mblock](/examples/line8/mblock/ex01_hear_line.mblock) | [ex01_hear_line.ino](/examples/line8/mblock/ex01_hear_line/ex01_hear_line.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  play tone ((440) + ((Pathfinder port [1 v] fine line position :: #9300DB) * (2))) Hz for (0.1) seconds :: sound
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Pathfinder 8-Way × mBlock 5  Example 1: Hear where the line is  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot port 1. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port1(1);           // sensor on mBot port 1
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port1.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    buzzer.tone((440 + (mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x02) * 2)), 100);   // Pitch = 440 + fine line position × 2 Hz, for 0.1 s
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Pitch = 440 + fine line position × 2 Hz, for 0.1 s

**What you should see**: Black line under the centre of the sensor: 440 Hz. Slide the line to the left and the pitch drops (240 Hz at the far left); to the right it rises (640 Hz at the far right). Remove the line and the pitch stays where the line was last seen.

**FAQ**
- **No sound?** → The buzzer is on the board and is not loud; listen closely, or change 0.1 s to 0.3 s.
- **Pitch goes the wrong way?** → Left and right are seen from behind the robot, facing forward. Mounting the sensor rotated 180° reverses it.
- **"Line width" is still 0 on the black line?** → Not calibrated yet: calibrate once with the button on the sensor (see "Before you start").
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 1), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 2: The LED shows which side the line is on

**What this example does**: Use "if… then… else…" on the line position: left = red, right = blue, centre = green; line width 0 (no line) = LED off. This is the skeleton of every line follower; the next example just swaps the LED for the wheels.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- Pathfinder 8-Way (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board
- A white mat with a black line (about 2 cm wide)

**Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1**. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex02_led_side.mblock](/examples/line8/mblock/ex02_led_side.mblock) | [ex02_led_side.ino](/examples/line8/mblock/ex02_led_side/ex02_led_side.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line width :: #9300DB) = (0)&gt; then
    LED [all v] colour red (0) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
  else
    if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line position :: #9300DB) &lt; (-2)&gt; then
      LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
    else
      if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line position :: #9300DB) &gt; (2)&gt; then
        LED [all v] colour red (0) green (0) blue (255) :: looks
      else
        LED [all v] colour red (0) green (255) blue (0) :: looks
      end
    end
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Pathfinder 8-Way × mBlock 5  Example 2: The LED shows which side the line is on  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot port 1. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port1(1);           // sensor on mBot port 1
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port1.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x03) == 0)) {   // If the line width = 0 (no line)
      rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // No line: LED off
    } else {
      if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x01) < -2)) {   // Otherwise, if the line position is less than -2 (left)
        rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // Line to the left: red
      } else {
        if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x01) > 2)) {   // Otherwise, if the line position is greater than 2 (right)
          rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 0, 255); rgbled.show();   // Line to the right: blue
        } else {
          rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 255, 0); rgbled.show();   // Line in the centre: green
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If the line width = 0 (no line)
      - No line: LED off
      - otherwise:
         - Otherwise, if the line position is less than -2 (left)
            - Line to the left: red
            - otherwise:
               - Otherwise, if the line position is greater than 2 (right)
                  - Line to the right: blue
                  - otherwise:
                     - Line in the centre: green

**What you should see**: Line in the centre: green. Move it more than 2 channels to the left: red; to the right: blue. On plain white the LED goes off.

**FAQ**
- **How do I change the colours?** → Edit the three red/green/blue numbers (0~255); 255, 255, 0 is yellow, for example.
- **"Line width" is still 0 on the black line?** → Not calibrated yet: calibrate once with the button on the sensor (see "Before you start").
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 1), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 3: The line position drives one wheel

**What this example does**: Divide the "fine line position" (−100 to +100) by 2 and use it directly as the left wheel power: line on the right → forward, on the left → backward, centre → still; the further off, the faster. Prop the robot up (wheels off the ground) to watch one wheel follow the line, then put it down in the next example.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Pathfinder 8-Way (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board
- A white mat with a black line (about 2 cm wide)

**Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1**. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex03_one_wheel.mblock](/examples/line8/mblock/ex03_one_wheel.mblock) | [ex03_one_wheel.ino](/examples/line8/mblock/ex03_one_wheel/ex03_one_wheel.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  left wheel power ((Pathfinder port [1 v] fine line position :: #9300DB) / (2)) %, right wheel power (0) % :: motion
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Pathfinder 8-Way × mBlock 5  Example 3: The line position drives one wheel  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot port 1. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port1(1);           // sensor on mBot port 1
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port1.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    wheels((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x02) / 2), 0);   // Left wheel power = fine line position ÷ 2 (−50 to +50), right wheel 0
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Left wheel power = fine line position ÷ 2 (−50 to +50), right wheel 0

**What you should see**: Line in the centre: the left wheel is still. Move the line right: the left wheel turns forward, faster the further off; move it left: the wheel reverses.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **The wheel creeps with the line in the centre?** → The fine position is not always exactly 0. Add "if line width = 0 or the absolute value is below 6 then power 0" to hold still.
- **"Line width" is still 0 on the black line?** → Not calibrated yet: calibrate once with the button on the sensor (see "Before you start").
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 1), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 4: Three-way line following

**What this example does**: Swap the LED of example 2 for the wheels: line on the left → left wheel slow, right wheel fast (steer left); on the right the opposite; in the centre both wheels equal. The robot wiggles along the black line: the simplest line follower and the easiest to understand.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Pathfinder 8-Way (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board
- A white mat with a black line (about 2 cm wide)

**Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1**. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex04_three_way.mblock](/examples/line8/mblock/ex04_three_way.mblock) | [ex04_three_way.ino](/examples/line8/mblock/ex04_three_way/ex04_three_way.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line position :: #9300DB) &lt; (-2)&gt; then
    left wheel power (10) %, right wheel power (40) % :: motion
  else
    if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line position :: #9300DB) &gt; (2)&gt; then
      left wheel power (40) %, right wheel power (10) % :: motion
    else
      left wheel power (30) %, right wheel power (30) % :: motion
    end
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Pathfinder 8-Way × mBlock 5  Example 4: Three-way line following  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot port 1. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port1(1);           // sensor on mBot port 1
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port1.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x01) < -2)) {   // If the line position is less than -2 (left)
      wheels(10, 40);   // Line to the left: left wheel slow, right wheel fast, steer left
    } else {
      if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x01) > 2)) {   // Otherwise, if the line position is greater than 2 (right)
        wheels(40, 10);   // Line to the right: left wheel fast, right wheel slow, steer right
      } else {
        wheels(30, 30);   // Line in the centre: both wheels equal, straight ahead
      }
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If the line position is less than -2 (left)
      - Line to the left: left wheel slow, right wheel fast, steer left
      - otherwise:
         - Otherwise, if the line position is greater than 2 (right)
            - Line to the right: left wheel fast, right wheel slow, steer right
            - otherwise:
               - Line in the centre: both wheels equal, straight ahead

**What you should see**: The robot wiggles its way along the black line. If it flies off on sharp bends, lower the 40 and change the 10 to 0.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **"Line width" is still 0 on the black line?** → Not calibrated yet: calibrate once with the button on the sensor (see "Before you start").
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 1), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 5: Proportional line following + stop when the line is lost

**What this example does**: Three-way following keeps wiggling. This example uses "fine line position × 0.3" as the steering force: a little off = a little turn, far off = a big turn, so the drive is smoother. Line width detects a lost line: no line → stop with a red LED, following normally → green. This is the starting point for competition line followers.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Pathfinder 8-Way (Makeblock edition) + mBot socket board
- A white mat with a black line (about 2 cm wide)

**Wiring**: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot **port 1**. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex05_p_follow.mblock](/examples/line8/mblock/ex05_p_follow.mblock) | [ex05_p_follow.ino](/examples/line8/mblock/ex05_p_follow/ex05_p_follow.ino) |

<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;(Pathfinder port [1 v] line width :: #9300DB) = (0)&gt; then
    stop moving :: motion
    LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
  else
    set [turn v] to ((Pathfinder port [1 v] fine line position :: #9300DB) * (0.3))
    left wheel power ((30) + (turn)) %, right wheel power ((30) - (turn)) % :: motion
    LED [all v] colour red (0) green (255) blue (0) :: looks
  end
end</pre>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Pathfinder 8-Way × mBlock 5  Example 5: Proportional line following + stop when the line is lost  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Pathfinder → mBot socket board → mBot port 1. Mount it under the front of the robot about 1 cm above the ground, facing straight down.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port1(1);           // sensor on mBot port 1
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer
float turn = 0;               // variable：turn

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port1.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if ((mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x03) == 0)) {   // If the line width = 0 (no line)
      wheels(0, 0);   // No line: stop
      rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // Red LED
    } else {
      turn = (mbcRead(mbc_port1, 0x02) * 0.3);   // turn = fine line position × 0.3 (−30 to +30)
      wheels((30 + turn), (30 - turn));   // Left = 30 + turn, right = 30 − turn: line on the left (negative) → left wheel slow, right wheel fast
      rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 255, 0); rgbled.show();   // Green LED
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the sensor to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If the line width = 0 (no line)
      - No line: stop
      - Red LED
      - otherwise:
         - turn = fine line position × 0.3 (−30 to +30)
         - Left = 30 + turn, right = 30 − turn: line on the left (negative) → left wheel slow, right wheel fast
         - Green LED

**What you should see**: The robot follows the black line smoothly with a green LED; lift it off the line and it stops at once with a red LED. If it still wiggles on straights, lower 0.3 (e.g. 0.2); if it cannot make the bends, raise it.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **Does it stop at crossings too?** → No, at a crossing the line width gets larger, not 0. To stop at crossings, try "line width > 5" instead of "= 0".
- **"Line width" is still 0 on the black line?** → Not calibrated yet: calibrate once with the button on the sensor (see "Before you start").
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 1), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.
